findings.title: Google refresh stores the safeParse result object as the credential key
findings.body: `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns the zod `SafeParseReturnType` (`{ success, data }`), not the parsed value (see `_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts:29`). Line 97 assigns that to `key`, and line 100 writes it to `prisma.credential.update({ data: { key } })`. The old code stored `googleCredentialSchema.parse(...)`, which was the credentials object itself. After the first token refresh, every Google Calendar credential holds `{ success: true, data: {...} }`. The next `googleAuth` call runs `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` on line 75, which throws, so Google Calendar breaks for every user whose token expires. This happens with credential sharing off, which is the default. Use `.data` after checking `.success`.

findings.title: `minimumTokenResponseSchema` computed keys collapse to "[object Object]" and the schema strips the expiry
findings.body: `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` are evaluated as property names. A Zod type has no custom `toString`, so both are `"[object Object]"`. The second key overwrites the first, and the schema becomes `{ access_token: string, "[object Object]": unknown? }`. The comment says that any numeric property is treated as the expiry, but nothing enforces that. `z.object` strips unknown keys by default, so `expires_in`, `expiry_date` and `token_type` are dropped from `data` in sync mode. Callers then compute with `undefined`. In `zoomvideo/lib/VideoApiAdapter.ts:122`, `Math.round(Date.now() + undefined * 1000)` is `NaN`, which is saved as `expiry_date`. The next `zoomTokenSchema.safeParse(oldCredential.key)` on line 113 then fails with "Invalid credentials were saved in the DB". Use `z.object({ access_token: z.string() }).passthrough()` plus an explicit check that an expiry field exists, or use `.catchall(z.unknown())`.

findings.title: Placeholder refresh_token "refresh_token" overwrites the real stored token, also with credential sharing off
findings.body: When the response has no `refresh_token`, the code sets `data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"` on every call, not only in sync mode. In `office365calendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:264` the code does `{ ...o365AuthCredentials, ...tokenResponse.data }`. `refreshTokenResponseSchema` (line 56) declares `refresh_token` optional, because Microsoft may omit it. Previously the stored refresh token survived that merge. Now it is replaced by the literal string `"refresh_token"`, and the next refresh fails with `invalid_grant`. This breaks Office 365 Calendar for self-hosters who don't use credential sharing. Apply the placeholder only in sync mode, or don't mutate the data at all and let callers keep the stored token.

findings.title: In sync mode the raw fetch Response is returned to callers that expect other shapes
findings.body: The non-sync branch returns whatever `refreshFunction` returns: an axios response with `.data` (zohocrm, zoho-bigin), a hubspot token object, or a gaxios `res` with `.data` (google). The sync branch returns a fetch `Response`. These callers read `zohoCrmTokenInfo.data.error` (`zohocrm/lib/CalendarService.ts:217`), `tokenInfo.data.error` (`zoho-bigin/lib/CalendarService.ts:96`), `res?.data` (`googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:94`) and `hubspotRefreshToken.expiresIn` (`hubspot/lib/CalendarService.ts:192`). On a `Response`, `.data` is undefined, so this throws a TypeError or yields NaN expiries. Hubspot and Zoho swallow the error with `log.error`, so the user gets no token and no visible error. Only the fetch-based callers (zoom, webex, office365, lark) happen to fit. Make `refreshOAuthTokens` return the shape the non-sync path returns, for example by parsing the JSON and wrapping it as `{ data }` or by letting each caller adapt. Also, the POST to `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` carries no auth header or secret, so any caller that can reach the endpoint can request tokens for any `calcomUserId`. Consider sending `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` or a similar header.

findings.title: `prisma` is used but never imported in the Salesforce service
findings.body: The file imports nothing from `@calcom/prisma` (the only `prisma` match in the file is line 96). `getClient` therefore throws a `ReferenceError` on every construction, which breaks all Salesforce calendar and CRM operations. It also fails type-checking.

findings.title: Salesforce now does a token refresh on every service construction, ignores the new token, and bypasses refreshOAuthTokens
findings.body: `getClient` previously only built a `jsforce.Connection` with the stored `refreshToken`, so jsforce refreshed lazily. It now POSTs to login.salesforce.com every time the service is constructed. That adds a network round trip to each booking, and it risks Salesforce rate limits. It also calls `fetch` directly rather than `refreshOAuthTokens`, so credential sharing is not honored for this app. Line 106 then builds the connection with the old `credentialKey.access_token` instead of `accessTokenParsed.data.access_token`, which makes the refresh pointless for this connection. Separately, `response.statusText !== "OK"` is a brittle success check. `parseRefreshTokenResponse` throws on a failed parse, so the `!accessTokenParsed.success` branch on line 92 is dead. Route this through `refreshOAuthTokens` only when the token is expired. Use the new access token for the connection.

findings.title: Bigin passes the credential id where `refreshOAuthTokens` expects the user id
findings.body: The third parameter of `refreshOAuthTokens` is `userId: number | null`. Here `credentialId` is passed. In sync mode the endpoint is asked for tokens for `calcomUserId = <credential id>`, which is a different, arbitrary user. That fetches or writes another user's credentials, and the credential is saved from that response. `biginAuth` has the credential in scope, so pass `credential.userId`. `refreshAccessToken` needs it as a parameter, because it currently receives only `credentialId`.

findings.title: Unrelated change replaces `appConfig.slug` with a hardcoded string
findings.body: The redirect URI used `appConfig.slug` (still imported and used on lines 12 and 22) and is now hardcoded to `zoho-bigin`. It has nothing to do with this feature, and it creates a second source of truth for the slug. Revert it.

findings.title: Webhook secret is compared with `!==`, and the endpoint has no method check
findings.body: The secret check is a plain string comparison, so it is not constant-time. Use `crypto.timingSafeEqual` on equal-length buffers. The handler also accepts any HTTP method. The endpoint overwrites stored OAuth credentials, so restrict it to POST.

findings.title: Invalid body, bad ciphertext or bad JSON produce an unhandled 500 instead of a 4xx
findings.body: `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse` (line 31), `symmetricDecrypt` and `JSON.parse` (lines 57-59) all throw on bad input. Nothing catches the error, so the caller gets a generic 500, and a zod error may leak details. Use `safeParse` and a try/catch that returns 400. The decrypted `keys` is also written straight into `credential.key` without any validation against the app's key shape.

findings.title: Dead `tokenResponse.success` check and the removed error log
findings.body: `parseRefreshTokenResponse` throws when the parse fails. After it returns, `tokenResponse.success` is always true, so `tokenResponse.success && tokenResponse.data` is dead. The `console.error` that logged the ZodError and the Microsoft response was removed, and the thrown error `Invalid refreshed tokens were returned` carries neither. That loses the diagnostic detail, and an invalid response now aborts instead of being tolerated.
